newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian president left with few Western friends.
newsitem.headline: Albanian president left with few Western friends.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha, who won accolades in the early 1990s but is now cold-shouldered by the international community, has his reputation, if not his job, on the line in general elections on Sunday.

Initially the West's darling for dragging Albania out of Stalinist isolation and preaching market values, Berisha stands accused of failing to foresee the collapse of shady investment schemes that triggered months of insurrection in the poor Balkan state.
Many Albanians who voted for his Democratic Party in two previous elections now blame him for their misfortune and see the vote as a way to pass judgement on his five years in power.
Berisha is not up for re-election. But he has campaigned hard to keep the huge majority his Democrats won in a general election a year ago now widely seen to have been discredited by irregularities.
He is unrepentant in accusing the Socialists, the reformed inheritors of Albania's hardline communists, of instigating the recent uprising, which has left 1,500 dead.
"You and your brothers are understandably upset by gang violence. I pledge to you that on June 29 these gangs will meet an ugly end," Berisha said in the campaign's final week.
"We are going to destroy the lies of the Socialist leaders who work with paid gangsters. We are going down the path of God, democracy and well-being."

Berisha, a 52-year-old former university cardiologist, first took office in April 1992. He won lavish praise from Washington for keeping cool while Bosnia in adjacent former Yugoslavia was engulfed in war and U.S. military advisers and aid poured into the country.
Economically, Berisha made all the right noises. He won the confidence of foreign governments and international lending institutions over his plans to introduce real economic reform.
Speaking fluent English and French, Berisha sounded every bit the new Albanian leader, embracing Western values and seeking closer ties with NATO and the European Union.
But his image was battered by charges that his party's election victory last year was unfair and by the collapse of the pyramid schemes.
Berisha acknowledged that his government had failed to heed warnings from the International Monetary Fund and World Bank to check the proliferation of dubious investment funds.
Facing rising opposition, he resorted increasingly to authoritarian means, banning demonstrations and then imposing a state of emergency on March 2 when the revolt turned sharply worse in the south.
A day later, Berisha engineered his own re-election unopposed by a parliament controlled by the Democrats.
With Albania on the brink of complete anarchy for two days, its police and army nowhere to be seen, Western envoys shuttled to Tirana to persuade Berisha to make concessions.
He eventually agreed to Sunday's early election and to the appointment of a multi-party government to stage it.
Berisha co-founded the Democratic Party in December 1990 after a student revolt forced President Ramiz Alia's Stalinist government to allow political parties and free elections.
He had worked inside a communist system that permitted him to study in France. But he has denied that he was a member of the medical team that administered to high-ranking Stalinists.
The Democrats plucked him from among several contenders to lead the party in 1991 and he scored a landslide election win a year later.
Berisha remained popular until a referendum in 1994 in which a narrow majority of Albanians rejected a draft constitution which would have given the president more power.
Opposition parties say the mood then changed.

Berisha was shunned by foreign leaders after last year's election irregularities became apparent. He came under fire for the jailing of Socialist Party leader Fatos Nano, on corruption charges which Western monitors regarded as politically motivated.
Berisha pardoned and released Nano at the height of the March turmoil.
